10439-from-yauco-to-las-marias-a-recent-:
Karl Stephen Herrman wrote this campaign history of the Independent Regular Brigade under Brigadier General Schwan in Puerto Rico. The book follows American regular troops from Yauco to Las Marias during the Spanish-American War, day by day and march by march. Herrman writes as a participant close to officers and men.

Chapters treat the brigade's make-up, the first day's march to Sabana Grande, the people of Puerto Rico, and the move to San German against an approaching Spanish force. Hard tack, wayside hospitality, and smoke-talks fill the gaps between battles. Readers get a detailed, soldier's-eye account of a short, sharp campaign.
10551-affair-in-araby:
Talbot Mundy opens this Arabian adventure with a chess image. A king matters little while your side wins, but becomes a source of anxiety when you start to lose. The narrator, an American who loves a good fight, admits he is told he ought to be ashamed of fighting for a king. Yet he notes his critics fight just as hard with tongues. The tone is brisk, worldly, and comic.

The plot promises a hoist for the Feisul boy, with Arab politics, desert warfare, and British intrigue in the background. Mundy, master of Eastern adventure, writes with pace and local color. Readers get a lively, post-war tale of Arabia, kings, and the game of empire.
12424-the-trail-of-the-tramp-by-a-no-1-t:
A-No. 1, the famous tramp who claimed to have traveled five hundred thousand miles for seven dollars and sixty-one cents, wrote The Trail of the Tramp from actual experiences of his own life. Illustrated by Joseph Earl Shrock, the eighth edition sold for twenty-five cents from the A-No. 1 Publishing Company in Erie, Pennsylvania.

The book tells how tramps ride trains, beg food, dodge police, and keep a code of the road. A mid-book scene has a boy slip a timepiece into his pocket under fear of punishment, then join Danny at a door where a lady hands over a bright silver dollar. A-No. 1 writes with humor and defiance, celebrating freedom from work and rent. The book is a rare tramp autobiography, romanticizing a hard life.
15306-the-mirrors-of-downing-street-some:
Harold Begbie, writing as a Gentleman with a Duster, offers political reflections in The Mirrors of Downing Street, published by Putnam in 1921. A portrait of David Lloyd George fronts the book, and a John Morley motto on right and wrong in the nature of things sets the tone. Publishers note that Britain and America fought together and won the war.

Begbie reflects on ministers, power, and character in postwar Britain, with a moralist's eye for vanity and duty. The sketches mix praise and warning, never mere party talk. Readers of political portraiture will find the book sharp, earnest, and rooted in its moment.
15857-critical-strictures-on-the-new-tra:
A short critical pamphlet from 1763, by James Boswell, Andrew Erskine, and George Dempster, on David Malloch's new tragedy Elvira. The Augustan Reprint Society reissued it as publication number thirty-five, with an introduction by Frederick A. Pottle. The Clark Memorial Library at the University of California published the reprint in 1952. Three young Scots wits attack a fashionable play.

Boswell, later Johnson's biographer, joins Erskine and Dempster in mocking Elvira's plot, verse, and feeling. Their strictures mix learning with laughter, quoting the play to damn it. The pamphlet shows Augustan criticism at its liveliest: sharp, social, and unafraid of names. Scholars still read it for Boswell's early voice and for the theatre wars of 1763.
16608-bruvver-jim-s-baby:
Philip Verrill Mighels tells a Nevada mining-camp tale in this 1904 novel, dedicated to his mother. It opens on a bright November day of the Indian rabbit drive, as Piute hunters sweep a sage-brush valley. A mighty little hunter, Jim's discoveries, a doll, a cabin Christmas, and a blizzard follow, with gold in Borealis and a day of joy to close.

Mighels writes with humor and heart, in the dialect flavor of the camps. Old Jim's resolution and the baby's fortunes drive the story. Readers of western fiction will find a gentle, funny tale of rough men softened by a child, in the best camp-story tradition.
16856-sermons-at-rugby:
John Percival, bishop of Hereford and once headmaster of Rugby, wrote these sermons at Rugby, issued by James Nisbet in London in 1905. An introductory note calls them stray chips from a busy schoolmaster's workshop, gathered by a kind publisher and set in his chosen order. They claim no continuous doctrine; seasons, term beginnings and endings, or school incidents suggested each one.

Percival speaks to boys growing toward their endless life, and to masters who teach them. His sermons mix school life with Christian teaching in plain, earnest terms. The book gives a warm, first-hand view of a great headmaster's pulpit, useful for readers of school history and of Victorian church life.
20693-the-jungle-baby:
The Jungle Baby is a story for children about a baby growing up among animals at a jungle home. The household includes a cat, Mioux-Mioux, and a dog, Wooff-Wooff, who treat the child as their own charge. The baby, called Bab-ba, loves the birds that visit the garden.

Mioux-Mioux used to watch the birds out of the corner of her eyes. She never tried to catch them, because she knew Bab-ba loved them. Wooff-Wooff sat with his head on one side, wondering how the birds managed with only two legs. The tale charms by keeping the animals' manners true.
21904-the-millionaire-baby:
A child is missing, and a fortune hangs on her, in Anna Katharine Green's The Millionaire Baby, published in 1905. The narrator, a young man supporting a mother and two sisters, begins in deep discouragement before the morning papers change his day. Two little shoes open the tale. A voice in the frontispiece insists the child is dead, and that this must be understood between the speakers.

Green, author of The Leavenworth Case, builds the mystery through chalk marks, an old house in Yonkers, and a secret pavilion. Chapters promise espionage, a phantom, and a final struggle. Her plots were famous for holding the solution to the last act. This late novel keeps her machinery oiled: wealth, a vanished heir, and quiet people with loud secrets.
22212-the-paternoster-ruby:
Charles Edmonds Walk wrote The Paternoster Ruby, a detective novel published in 1910. Walk had already made his name with The Silver Blade and The Yellow Circle. His title names a great red gem. The frontispiece shows the ruby between two people, a splash of crimson flame. Meanwhile the crowd of a London station rushes past in the opening pages.

A stolen jewel, a murder, and a trail through London society drive the plot. Walk builds his mystery in the manner of the new century's detective tales. Contemporary readers took the book as a rattling yarn of crime and pursuit. It survives as a neat sample of pre-war popular detection.
22881-my-friend-bobby:
A small child's voice tells My Friend Bobby. Bobby goes outdoors even when it is cold, the narrator explains. Mother says the child should not play with Bobby so much, since Bobby is, after all, only a dog. But Bobby is the right size in a world of giants.

Everyone else is so big, the child says. When parents are home, all that shows is their legs, unless you look way up high. Doing something bad is scary when the grown-ups are so big and strong. Through those simple observations the story builds a child's whole moral world. It is a tender, funny piece of child-eye storytelling, and its honesty about fear gives it weight.
25564-the-water-babies-a-fairy-tale-for-:
Charles Kingsley writes this fairy tale for a land baby, first published in 1863 and reprinted here in 1922 with colour pictures by Warwick Goble. A dragonfly, king of all the flies, whirring up and hanging poised on its wings, fronts the book.

Once upon a time, a little chimney sweep sets the story going, and the tale follows a child cleaned and changed by water into a new life among water creatures. Kingsley dedicates the book to his youngest son Grenville Arthur and to all other good little boys, mixing wonder, natural history, and moral teaching.
2693-greyfriars-bobby:
Eleanor Atkinson tells the true tale of Greyfriars Bobby, a little Skye terrier bred on a heathery Pentland slope. When the time gun booms from Edinburgh Castle, Bobby yelps, the youngest and smallest and shaggiest of his litter, come to market with Auld Jock, a farm laborer.

After Jock's death, Bobby keeps vigil at his grave in Greyfriars churchyard through rain, snow, and hunger, fed by kindly townsfolk. Atkinson writes with deep feeling about loyalty that outlasts death. The book remains a beloved animal classic, and the story behind Edinburgh's famous little statue.
27201-woman-on-her-own-false-gods-and-th:
Eugène Brieux's Woman on Her Own, False Gods, and The Red Robe, published by Brentano's in 1916, gathers three plays in English versions by Mrs. Bernard Shaw, J. F. Fagan, and A. Bernard Miall, with an introduction by Brieux. Woman on Her Own, La Femme Seule, leads the volume.

Its heroine Thérèse leads workwomen who refuse overtime cuts and demand a separate workshop, while socialists warn that women in the factory undercut men's wages. The women answer they will take the men's places, making the play a sharp drama of labor, sex, and solidarity.
28226-the-war-in-the-air-vol-1-the-part-:
Walter Raleigh wrote The War in the Air, volume one, Oxford, 1922, as the official history of the Royal Air Force in the Great War. Raleigh, working from official documents by direction of the Historical Section, traces flight from the first free aeroplane flight of December 17, 1903, to the air force Britain built by 1918. The Clarendon Press published the volume.

Chapters cover the conquest of the air, pioneers, machines, and the new uses of aircraft: reconnaissance, artillery spotting, photography, bombing, and naval patrol. Raleigh stresses men of science and men of action alike. The book gives a solid, official account of air war's birth.
29380-the-adventures-of-herr-baby:
Mrs. Molesworth's children's tale, first printed in 1881 and reprinted by Macmillan in 1895, follows a boy of four, Herr Baby, through a string of small wonders. Pictures by Walter Crane fill the book. The chapters take him inside a trunk, up early in the morning, away by land and sea, into an old shop with an ogre, and at last to a secret found. The verse from Wordsworth on the title page sets the tone: a fair, fresh child of five, seen with fond eyes.

Molesworth writes for young listeners, with gentle humor and a firm sense of a child's logic. Each chapter is a short, self-contained jaunt, easy to read aloud at bedtime. Fans of Victorian children's books will find a tender, old-style classic that still charms in its small, brave hero.
31118-the-long-day-the-story-of-a-new-yo:
Published by the Century Company in 1905, The Long Day tells a New York working girl's life in her own voice, without naming her. Sixteen chapters and an epilogue follow her arrival in the city, her search for work, and light housekeeping in a Fourteenth Street lodging house. They go on to box-making learned from Phoebe and a dangerous friendship with Henrietta Manners.

Later chapters take her into a home for working girls, four weeks making artificial flowers, and work as a shaker in a steam laundry. The book is dedicated to three lady-friends beside her: Minnie, Bessie, and Eunice. Plain and unsparing, it remains a classic firsthand account of what a working girl's long day actually cost.
31599-to-remember-charlie-by:
Roger Dee's story, as its headnote puts it, is about Charlie, a one-eyed dog, and Joey, a crippled boy. Between them, perhaps, the headnote says, they changed the face of the universe. The narrator nearly stumbles over Joey in the dark. His wheelchair is parked on the strip of grass between his mother's trailer and the one the narrator shares with Doc Shull. Joey usually sits where he can look across the Twin Palms trailer court toward the Tampa highway.

The headnote frames the tale with the claim that simple faith can alter the scheme of the universe. Scientists and historians, it says, dismiss strange events as supernatural or miracle. Dee's story follows a boy, a dog, and a quiet faith that proves larger than the material world around them.
32613-tabby:
Winston Marks's Tabby, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in March 1954, begins as letters from an island expedition. Fred writes to Ben about nine expedition members, a lazy replacement named Cleveland, a comfortable camp, and a screened lab that has solved the insect nuisance.

Then a saucer-like craft lands offshore, about six feet wide and eight inches deep, topped by a small dome. Its lid pops open as the men row near, and Marks turns a paradise atoll into a scene of growing menace, as a little green fly called Tabby proves far from harmless.
33575-the-comedies-of-carlo-goldoni-edit:
Helen Zimmern edited this 1892 collection of Carlo Goldoni's comedies, with an introduction and a sonnet by Robert Browning. Browning praises Goldoni as the good, gay, sunniest of souls who glassed half of Venice in his verse. Four plays follow: A Curious Mishap, The Beneficent Bear, The Fan, and The Spendthrift Miser. Voltaire's praise, quoted in the introduction, called Goldoni a painter and son of nature.

Zimmern explains Goldoni's chief merit: he freed the Italian theatre from artificial pantomime performances and, together with Molière, laid the foundations of modern drama. The comedies throng with Venetian people on piazzas, streets, and bridges, speaking soft language in bright dress. The volume is an inviting entry to Goldoni for readers of classic comedy and Italian theatre history.
33777-tom-brown-at-rugby:
Thomas Hughes, writing as an Old Boy, tells the classic school story Tom Brown at Rugby in this Ginn edition for children, edited by Clara Weaver Robinson. The introduction argues that the true aim of education is the right development of character: children should gain knowledge and sound habits of thought, but above all become honest, steadfast, and manly. Dr. Arnold, headmaster of Rugby, succeeded eminently at that object, the editor writes.

Hughes caught and immortalized the spirit of Arnold's work, emphasizing the moral earnestness of his pupils without cant. Notes prepared for grammar-school children accompany the text, a few passages were omitted to suit American schoolboys, and typographical errors of former editions were corrected. The book remains the model school story: games, friendships, bullying faced down, and a boy growing into honor under a great teacher.
34711-the-life-of-roger-langdon-told-by-:
Roger Langdon, station-master at Silverton on the Great Western Railway, told the story of his own life, and his daughter Ellen added to it after his death on July 18, 1894. Whitaker's Almanack for 1895 praised him in its survey of astronomy: a self-taught man who ground an eight-inch silver-on-glass mirror on a machine of his own making. In 1872 he had sent the Royal Astronomical Society a paper on the markings of Venus.

The memoir begins with childhood beatings, a kind old mother, and the question he kept asking himself: why was I born? Chapters carry him through a secret departure, years in Jersey, return and marriage, and at last his scientific work. It is the record of a working man who made himself an astronomer in his spare hours. Elliot Stock published the book in London.
34807-what-was-the-gunpowder-plot-the-tr:
John Gerard, a priest of the Society of Jesus, wrote this probe of the Gunpowder Plot. Its full head states its method in plain words: the tale as it is oft told, put to the test of the first proof. The old spell of the days of the plot is kept in the bits the book quotes. A cut of the plot stands at its front. It was printed at London by Osgood, McIlvaine and their house.

The theme needs no gloss. In 1605 a set of men laid kegs of powder in a vault of the houses of rule, to blow up the King and the men of state at one stroke. The tale of that plot, as schools and sheets tell it, is a fixed thing by now.
35254-in-the-onyx-lobby:
In the Onyx Lobby, a mystery tale by Carolyn Wells, bears a copyright of 1920. Wells had written The Man Who Fell Through the Earth and other tales of crime. The scene is the Campanile Apartment House in New York, between Columbus Circle and Times Square.

The house is proud of its ornate front and its onyx lobby, once the talk of the block. Sir Herbert Binney opens the tale by mocking a family feud run by two women. Chapters bring a tricky game, a scrawled message, and busy police. A little dinner, a set in the library, and a hunt for the women drive the plot. Names like Penny Wise and Zizi hint at the light touch Wells keeps even in a murder tale.
35553-the-anglican-friar-and-the-fish-wh:
A Novice wrote The Anglican Friar, and the Fish Which He Took by Hook and by Crook, a comic legend dedicated to all lovers of angling, published at London in 1851. An introduction in verse explains the plan. A preface in verse, the poet says, is perhaps the reverse of the common and vulgar way.

Of the friar's birthplace he never heard, though from the twang of the brogue he guesses old Erin. Some queer Irishman related the tale. He tried every bait to fish out further particulars, and every bait proved no use. Readers get a Victorian comic poem about a fishing cleric, told in jog-trot rhymes with pictures.
36739-the-strange-story-of-rab-ra-by:
Maurus Jókai's The Strange Story of Rab Ráby, in its third edition from Jarrold and Sons at London, pictures the old régime in Hungary under Emperor Joseph II, from 1780 to 1790. Emil Reich's preface states the frame: plot and principal persons rest on facts, and the manners and institutions of the time are faithfully reflected.

The story is one of those frightful miscarriages of justice that political motives breed, and Reich pairs it with the Dreyfus case of his own day. So that English readers not misjudge Hungary, he reminds them its constitution is older than Magna Charta. Austria, so called, is merely a conventional phrase for the countries in the Reichsrath.
38347-the-millionaire-baby:
Anna Katharine Green, author of The Leavenworth Case and The Filigree Ball, wrote The Millionaire Baby for Bobbs-Merrill in 1905. Arthur Keller supplied the pictures for the Indianapolis edition. Twenty-seven chapters run from Two Little Shoes to The Final Struggle.

The narrator, a hard pressed detective, reads that Philo Ocumpaugh offers five thousand dollars for word of his lost daughter. Gwendolen, age six, vanished on August the 16th from her home on the Hudson. A first chapter dated August eighteenth sets the hunt in motion, through an old house in Yonkers, a bungalow, and a secret pavilion. Chalk marks, a coral bead, and a hidden wall all play their parts.
39858-trilby:
George du Maurier, who wrote Peter Ibbetson, made his fame with this novel of art life in Paris. Harper held the rights of 1894, and a special limited edition in paper covers came out in 1899. Du Maurier drew the plates himself, as he did for Punch.

Trilby, a lovely artist's model with a fine voice and no ear, stands at the heart. Taffy, the Laird of Cockpen, and Little Billee form her circle of painter friends. The front plate cries: it was Trilby. A French song heads the book: alas, I know a love song, sad and gay by turns. Svengali, the dark musician who sways Trilby, made the tale a byword of its age.
40266-the-punster-s-pocket-book-or-the-a:
Bernard Blackmantle's The Punster's Pocket-Book, or The Art of Punning, enlarged, came from Sherwood, Gilbert and Piper at London in 1826. Robert Cruikshank supplied fourteen original designs, and the frontispiece shows George the Fourth, to whom the book is dedicated as patron, lover and judge of wit.

Blackmantle, author of The English Spy, addresses his readers as fellow punsters. He claims to have gathered all that matters for an understanding of the Merry Art, with examples by the most celebrated punsters of the day, many printed here for the first time. He begs fresh original puns and epigrams from the public, hoping to issue a like volume every year, and quotes Martial: give me the man that wisely cracks a jest or pun.
40349-the-chase-of-the-ruby:
The Chase of the Ruby is a novel by Richard Marsh, sold in a late print. Ads in the front push a yet more famed tale of his, The Beetle. Press praise in those ads calls that tale a work of stark fright. No year is shown in the front pages of the hosted text.

One press voice says the book is the kind you can not set down. A next says you rise just to check that no one stands past your chair. Drawings by an artist named Williamson dress the text of the tale. A gem at the core and a hunt for it drive the plot of the book. Marsh wrote shock tales that sold in vast runs in his age.
40844-the-diva-s-ruby:
The Diva's Ruby, a novel by F Marion Crawford, was published by Macmillan in 1908. It is a sequel to his Primadonna and to Fair Margaret. Pictures by J Montgomery Flagg go with the text. The story grows out of the world of opera singers built in the earlier books.

The first chapter opens on a secret. A ruby mine lies hidden in the hills near a remote city of Central Asia. Two chief families of the place share the secret and guard it with care. The knowledge passes from father to son across many generations. That guarded wealth drives the plot that follows.
42341-of-the-capture-of-ticonderoga-his-:
Of the Capture of Ticonderoga: His Captivity and Treatment by the British is Ethan Allen's own narrative of his Revolutionary War exploits, written by himself. The copy here is the fifth edition, printed at Burlington in 1849, with notes. The publishers stress that the text is given in Allen's plain language without alteration.

An introduction frames Allen as a commander the Vermont mountain people trusted completely. It calls him an unyielding advocate of the rights of man. The narrative itself covers the stroke that made his name, the surprise capture of Fort Ticonderoga, and his later captivity and harsh treatment at British hands. The edition presents the book as the truest portrait of Allen, worth more than anything written about him by others.
42702-passing-by:
Passing By, a novel by Maurice Baring, was published by Martin Secker of London in 1921. The book is cast as the diary of Godfrey Mellor, a clerk at Gray's Inn. Entries begin in December 1908. The diary form lets the story unfold in small daily touches rather than in chapters.

The Housmans leave for Egypt as the diary opens, and Mellor sees them off. Christmas takes him to an uncle and aunt, and the new year returns him to the office. The Housmans come home to a new house at Campden Hill and give a house warming dinner. A portrait of Mrs Housman by Walter Bell hangs in the drawing room, and music is promised for the night. Baring builds his London world from parties, letters, and small talk.
43146-turquoise-and-ruby:
Turquoise and Ruby, a school story by L T Meade, was published by Grosset and Dunlap of New York in 1906. Meade wrote many tales for girls, often set in schools. The scene here is Mrs Hazlitt's school, where the girls are casting tableaux from Tennyson's Dream of Fair Women. Every girl envies the part of Helen of Troy.

Honora Beverley, called Nora, flatly refuses the part. Helen, she says, was not a good woman, and she will have nothing to do with her. She offers to play Jephthah's daughter or Iphigenia instead. Her friend Cara Burt cannot move her. The great refusal of the first chapter sets Nora's firm, scrupulous temper against the pull of the school crowd.
4348-poor-dear-margaret-kirby:
Kathleen Norris gathered this volume of stories, the third in her collected works, around the title tale Poor, Dear Margaret Kirby. The contents also include Bridging the Years, The Tide-Marsh, What Happened to Alanna, The Friendship of Alanna, and Miss Mix, Kidnapper. Later stories bring Shandon Waters, Dr. Bates and Miss Sally, and Rosemary's Stepmother.

The title story opens with Margaret Kirby reflecting that she and her husband have been married nearly seven years. Norris writes domestic fiction with warmth and moral clarity, about marriages, children, and neighbors. The volume suits readers who enjoy linked short stories of family life, told without haste.
44219-the-incubator-baby:
Ellis Parker Butler spins a stork fable in The Incubator Baby, printed in New York and London in 1906. Funk and Wagnalls made the book. Preston draws the plates. Butler had writ Pigs Is Pigs. Chapter one opens in the garden of Paradise, where the babies grow.

On the sunniest slope of the garden the trees stand in long, pleasant rows, the tale begins. The air is always balmy, and the trees are in bloom with pink and white blossoms. From a distance the trees look like apple trees. Close at hand, you see that the blossoms are little bows and streamers of ribbon, and the boughs sway with many dimpled babies. Kind old storks walk up and down beneath the trees, looking upward. They watch for a baby ready to be carried away into the big, strange world. Only storks of mature age may carry the babies.
45307-riverby: Riverby is a book by John Burroughs, printed at Boston and New York by Houghton, Mifflin and Company. The hosted copy opens with a publisher's list of Burroughs's works, in which Riverby stands as one volume of a uniform set of eleven. Wake-Robin, Winter Sunshine, Locusts and Wild Honey, and Signs and Seasons stand beside it in that list. The same pages price the set in cloth and in finer bindings, in the manner of a collected edition of a living author's works.
47342-gadsby:
Ernest Vincent Wright wrote a story of over fifty thousand words without using the letter E, printed in Los Angeles in 1939. A portrait of Wright fronts the book, which he gives to youth. He argues that a child's brain starts working at birth. Thousands of dormant atoms in it hold a mystic gift for noticing adults and figuring out their acts.

Play itself trains thought, he says, since rules put a child out if he fails to think. On that basis Wright shows a band of bright young folks who find a champion. The man has boys and girls of his own and draws youth to him like a fly. The tale's true marvel stays its missing letter on every page.
47349-the-wild-garden-or-our-groves-and-:
The Wild Garden, by Robinson, stands here in its third edition of 1883. Murray printed it in London, with Scribner and Welford in New York. Alfred Parsons drew the pictures. Its long subtitle gives the thesis. Groves and gardens can be made beautiful by naturalising hardy exotic plants. Robinson calls it one way onwards from the dark ages of flower gardening. Bare borders in the London parks, he adds, could be remade the same way. His preface recalls years of pleading for hardy flowers. Nurserymen answered that no one could go back to the mixed border.

Robinson answered that a vast world of plant beauty lay shut out. Hardy plants from other lands could live in English ground if let alone. Colonies of poet's narcissus fill the front plate. The book founded a school of natural planting.
47579-birds-and-all-nature-vol-4-no-4-oc:
Birds and All Nature, volume four, number four, for October 1898, is an issue of a natural history magazine illustrated by colour photography. Its contents mix birds, beasts, and verse. The lead article, Ears, is by Watt, and a bird of paradise, the kingbird of paradise, follows. The peccary, the bottle-nose dolphin, and the tufted puffin each get their pages.

Shorter pieces include a new champion for the sparrow, the talk of animals, the butterfly, and the armadillo. Nature's Grotesque, the red-head duck, birds in garden and orchard, and goldenrod close the list, with poems on autumn and October. The Ears article opens on the air itself, an elastic fluid surrounding the earth. Motions of things, alive or not, set it vibrating almost without cease.
47603-birds-and-all-nature-vol-4-no-5-no:
Birds and All Nature, volume 4, number 5, is a magazine issue for November 1898. Its pride is color photographs of birds and beasts. Short prose and verse fill some forty pages, from Nature's Orchestra to a summary at the end.

Readers meet the sharp tailed grouse, tame bats, and the American otter. The skylark, the golden plover, and the Caspian tern each get a turn. One piece asks if animals can count, and one praises the love of drink in butterflies. Verse on a turkey, a small bird, and dead flowers breaks up the fact pieces. Nature fans get a bright, mixed monthly feast.
47728-birds-and-all-nature-vol-4-no-6-de:
Birds and All Nature for December 1898 is a monthly nature magazine number, volume four, number six, illustrated by colour photography. The contents range widely: the lion, the cactus, humming birds, the silk-worm and the skunk.

The opening article, Voices, asks how animals communicate and how human speech began. Ants converse with their antennae, bees pass the news of a lost queen by touch, and hares keep silent except in pain. The writer disputes Darwin's courtship theory of song and argues that utterance began in the pleasure of the creature making the sound. From digging grunts and hunting cries, he traces language growing sound by sound. The number is popular natural history of the 1890s at its most miscellaneous and earnest.
47755-birds-and-all-nature-vol-5-no-1-ja:
Birds and All Nature, volume 5, number 1, is a monthly issue for January 1899. Marble edits the serial in Chicago, where Mumford prints it. Forty plates by color photography fill each number, the banner says. It calls itself a guide to the study of bird life.

Tess leads the issue, a chimpanzee of human like mind. She was caught in Africa, raised with a small girl in Boston, and dressed as a child of three. She walked upright and ate with knife and fork. Then come the whippoorwill, the mountain lion, and the holly tree. Bees, the eagle, nuts, and the snapping turtle fill the mixed feast.
47801-birds-and-all-nature-vol-5-no-2-fe:
Birds and All Nature, volume five, number two, is the February 1899 issue, illustrated by colour photography. The contents open with ginger, by Albert Schneider of Northwestern University school of pharmacy. He quotes Shakespeare on ginger being hot in the mouth.

Ginger, he explains, is the underground stem of a reed like plant. Its leaf and flower stems rise three to six feet, with sword shaped leaves above. The plant is said to be native to southern Asia, though now rarely found wild. Other pieces treat sap action, Emerson and a woodpecker story, a crab eating opossum, and a geographic turtle. Washington and Lincoln, noses, the white ibis, owls, a peacock, and snowflakes follow. Readers get a winter nature monthly of plants, beasts, and birds.
48106-birds-and-all-nature-vol-6-no-3-oc:
Birds and All Nature for October of eighteen ninety nine is one issue of a nature monthly. The Mumford house in Chicago put the issue out with colour prints. This copy is the third number of the sixth volume of the run. Forests, as a lead essay by a Chicago plant scholar, open the issue.

Short pieces treat an oak, a sparrow chick, a thrush, and farm fowls in turn. The Grand Canyon, oil wells, and brook trout widen the range of the mix. Verse, tales, and lore notes fill gaps between the fact pieces. Colour prints made the set a prize for schools and home shelves. The tone is bright and plain, for young and old nature fans alike.
48261-birds-and-all-nature-vol-6-no-5-de:
Birds and All Nature was a monthly magazine illustrated by colour photography. This file holds the December 1899 issue, volume six, number five. The contents mix birds, plants, and verses for the season. Pieces treat the red-tailed hawk, the Maryland yellow-throat, the pileated woodpecker, and the lyre-bird. A study of the colour photograph explains the magazine's own novelty, since colour pictures were still a wonder in print.

The opening article, The Tramps of Birdland, is a fable. The birds meet in council one morning, chattering over a serious question. A red-eyed vireo complains that their yearly resolutions have nothing resolute about them. Wood thrush, towhee, song sparrow, and flycatchers nod assent. Other items treat coca, native woods, a wild cat, and Christmas. The issue closes with indexes to all six volumes, marking its place as a bound year of a popular nature magazine.
48298-birds-and-all-nature-vol-7-no-1-ja:
A monthly nature magazine fills this item: Birds and All Nature, volume seven, number one, for January 1900, edited by Marble and printed at Chicago. Its cover line promises forty illustrations by colour photography, and calls the magazine a guide to the study of nature, in two volumes a year.

Contents for January run from season to specimen. A verse on the month from Spenser opens it, and an old year and young year piece follows. Then come the Virginia rail, the blue-winged teal, and the yellow-headed blackbird, with a wise little bird and a grasshopper spider between. Cotton fabrics, liquid air, common minerals, and valuable ores vary the fare. The black squirrel, the weasel, the American bison, and mushrooms on benches close the list.
48331-birds-and-all-nature-vol-7-no-2-fe:
Birds and All Nature, volume seven, number two, for February 1900, is a nature magazine illustrated by color photography. Its contents mix birds, beasts, plants, and lessons for young readers. A baby heron leads the number, followed by the killdeer, the cinnamon teal, and the clapper rail.

The baby heron, properly a great blue heron, measures five feet ten inches across the wings, though not yet in adult dress. Other pieces treat cotton textiles, the gopher, the mink, and common minerals and valuable ores. A memorial marks the late Elliott Coues, and shorter items cover snow birds, licorice, a winter walk in the woods, and the scarlet painted cup, closing with Washington's Monument.
49278-the-soldier-and-death-a-russian-fo:
The Soldier and Death, a Russian folk tale told in English by Arthur Ransome, is dated January 1920 in the head. A soldier has served God and the Great Tzar for twenty five years. He has earned three dry biscuits, and he sets off to walk home, singing at the top of his voice.

Once alone on the high road, he starts to think. He had clothes and food in service, and now he may be hungry and cold. He meets a beggar and gives him one biscuit. Then he meets a second beggar, and gives him the next. A third old beggar waits at a bend in the road. Readers get a short folk tale built on giving, want, and what comes of a kind act.
51735-big-baby:
Big Baby is a science fiction story by Jack Sharkey, from Galaxy Magazine of April 1962. Gaughan illustrated the tale for the magazine in that issue. A blurb at its head says the baby was lonesome, helpless, and afraid in the story. It was not his fault, the blurb adds, that he was seven hundred feet tall.

The tale opens on a radar like screen, where a dancing green blip traces an erratic course. A technician cuts the switch and offers to show the trace again to his superior. Jerry Norcriss tilts his head in a brief, authoritative nod in reply on the page. Sharkey, a Galaxy regular of those years, builds the story on the pathos of the giant foundling. The seven hundred foot baby is a monster only by scale, and the tale asks what the world owes a child it cannot hold.
53621-the-complete-poems-of-francis-ledw:
The Complete Poems of Francis Ledwidge gathers the verse of an Irish soldier poet, with an introduction by Lord Dunsany. Jenkins published it at London in 1919. Ledwidge dedicates the book to his mother, the first singer he knew. Dunsany's introduction is dated June 1915, from his service with the Inniskilling Fusiliers.

The poems divide into songs of the fields and songs of peace. The field songs sing of linnets in cages, twilights in March, spring rain, and the hills of home. Old Irish heroes walk there too: the death of Ailill, the sorrow of Findebar, and the passing of Caoilte. One poem breathes pure joy in nature: the wet lipped wind stirs the hedge and kisses flowers drooped for rain. Golden bees stain the lilies' frills while the blackbird sings in the rainbow. Ledwidge was killed in the Great War. This book is his monument.
53828-new-york-journal-of-pharmacy-volum:
Volume one of the New York Journal of Pharmacy came out in 1852, by leave of the College of Pharmacy of the City of New York. Benjamin McCready led the work, with a board made up of men of the trade. The first words to readers set out why the journal was born.

The college sought to raise the skill and standing of druggists and to guard the trade from fraud and poor work. New York held hundreds of druggists and great labs where drugs were made at scale, yet finds were lost when each man kept his own notes. A shared journal would spread new facts, home and foreign, through the whole trade.
53864-the-story-of-a-baby:
The Story of a Baby, by Ethel Turner, was published in London in 1896 by Ward, Lock and Bowden. Turner dedicates the book to the best woman in the world, at Sydney. Fifteen chapters run from The Burden of It through Dot and Larrie Fall Out and The Little Mother, to Sullivan Wooster, Gentleman.

Chapter one opens on a red road, where Larrie has carried the baby a long way and says it is Dot's turn. Dot argues with spirit: what is the use of being six-foot-two if he cannot carry a baby? He is exactly twenty-one pounds, she says; she weighed him on the kitchen scales yesterday. Turner, the Australian author of Seven Little Australians, writes of a young pair and an infant in the bush.
56126-the-son-of-don-juan-an-original-dr:
Son of Don Juan is an original drama in three acts by Jose Echegaray, rendered into English by James Graham. The London edition of eighteen ninety five belongs to a cameo series of small books. A portrait of the author stands near the front. A sketch of Echegaray's life, by the translator, opens the volume. He was born in Madrid in eighteen thirty two, the sketch fixes.

The first three years of his life passed in the capital, it says. In eighteen thirty five his father took a new post and the family moved. The boy had excellent tutors and a kind, cultured father, the sketch adds. His progress in learning was great and rapid. From the first he showed a passion for mathematics, it notes. Other plays by him, such as Mariana, are listed in the series.
57860-a-manual-of-conchology-according-t:
A Manual of Conchology, by Thomas Wyatt, was published at New York in 1838. Harper and Brothers issued it from Cliff Street that year. The system laid down by Lamarck, with later gains by de Blainville, frames the work. Thirty six plates with more than two hundred types, drawn from the natural shell, illustrate it.

The manual is exemplified and arranged for the use of students, its title states. An introduction calls conchology a numerous and beautiful branch of natural history. It treats of the testaceous covering of animals, Wyatt writes in that opening. Perhaps none but the department of flora can vie with it, he claims for shells. Variety, symmetry of form, and finish win his praise for the study in that passage.
58533-forge-of-foxenby:
Goodyear wrote Forge of Foxenby, a school tale for Blackie at London. Whitwell illustrated the book, sold also at Glasgow and Bombay. The front plate of Forge's triumph was missing from the source copy. Contents open with the county schools' final in sport. The captain and a figure called the Octopus follow in the heads.

A rival school paper, and what followed the first number, come next. Rhymes and riddles and the plea of Peter Mawdster fill early chapters. A burglary and a fight on the bowling-green follow. Counting a goal too soon is as unwise as counting chickens, it warns. The merry men score goals and win glory in the middle contents. A gift-goal, a three-cornered tournament, and the winning of the cup close it. Goodyear gives school sport, print, and friendship at full gallop.
61962-the-holy-piby:
The Holy Piby is a scripture of the Athlyi faith, printed at Newark in 1924. Houses of the faith at Newark, in South Africa, and at Kingston in Jamaica share the printing. The book falls into four parts, named Athlyi, Aggregation, the Fact of the Apostles, and Precaution. Its text is cast in numbered verses, in the manner of the Bible.

The first chapter tells the creation in plain Genesis style. God made man on the sixth day for his glory, the text says. Adam and Eve, the book declares, were of a mixed complexion. A second chapter tells how God entered a dead body and walked the earth. He took the name Elijah and worked miracles among men. The Piby became a sacred text for Black churches in the Caribbean and beyond.
6254-john-enderby:
Lincolnshire gave England no stronger, prouder, or handsomer man than John Enderby, Parker declares, a man King Charles made a knight against his will. When the King comes to Boston town on fen drainage and more secret business, Enderby protests the honour. It sits beyond a poor man driven to many shifts, with hard times and heavy taxes behind him. Lord Rippingdale sneers at the refusal, but Enderby answers that the King may command his life, body and soul.

This short tale follows a plain Englishman through knighthood, marriage, and the small disasters of household life, including a lost horse, saddle, and wool that leave him fearing his wife's wrath. Friends urge him to rule his roost, yet his fears prove human and comic. Parker writes Enderby with warm humour, a sturdy hero more afraid of home than of kings.
64603-mignon-or-bootles-baby:
J S Winter wrote Mignon, a short tale put out in New York in 1885. Winter had won a name with tales of horse troops and of camp life. A line from Doctor Johnson heads the book, in praise of small books held with ease. Plates show the key scenes of the tale.

The tale opens past the hour of night in the mess room of a horse troop camp. Three men sit at cards in the rooms of the Scarlet Lancers at Idleminster. One calls for Bootles to take a hand at the game. Plates then show Bootles who lifts a small child with clumsy pride. He vows he can not send the weak thing to the work house. A Mrs Gray, a man named Lacy, and a race with death fill the plates that trace the plot.
65233-what-the-judge-saw-being-twenty-fi:
What the Judge Saw is a memoir by Judge Edward Abbott Parry, printed in London by Smith, Elder in 1912. Its subtitle runs: being twenty-five years in Manchester by one who has done it. Parry also wrote Judgments in Vacation and The Scarlet Herring. He dedicates the volume to his partner, comrade, and wife.

The contents walk his career. Farewell Manchester opens the book, then Home and student days. Called to the Bar and early memories of Manchester follow. Quarter sessions and the sentence of death bring the judge's bench into view. Judges of yesterday, first briefs, and alarums and excursions fill the middle. The compleat citizen, overtime, and Pharisees and publicans round out the set. Parry writes the law as a human trade, with a light pen and a full notebook of court and city.
66388-the-invasion-of-india-by-alexander:
The Invasion of India by Alexander the Great retells the famed march into India from the accounts of ancient writers. The head matter here first praises Bernier's Travels in the Mogul Empire, a companion work in the same series from Constable. That praise shows the care the series took with old travel texts.

Alexander's push into India is told through the eyes of those who wrote of it near the time. Battles, rivers, and kings of the Punjab fill the account. Maps and notes help the reader follow the route. Students of ancient war and of India alike get a direct path into the sources.
69008-the-chinese-exclusion-act-report-a:
The Chamber of Commerce of the State of New York reports on the Chinese Exclusion Act in a New York print of 1889. The report and resolutions were adopted in December 1889. The work fell to the committee on Foreign Commerce and the Revenue Laws.

A letter starts the whole case. Huntington wrote to Low on November 24, 1888, and Low laid the letter before the Chamber. The report prints that letter in full as the base of its search. In it, Huntington says most folk felt the act of Congress was an unworthy act. He pleads for the pride and honor of the government. Trade men then weigh his charge in form.
69852-westminster-abbey-the-last-days-of:
Westminster Abbey, The Last Days of the Monastery, by Westlake, custodian and minor canon of the Abbey, was first published at London in 1921. The book tells the monastery's final age through the life and times of Abbot John Islip, who lived from 1464 to 1532. A front list shows the author's other Westminster works.

Chapters explain how the great house was run, from the Rule of Saint Benedict to its fourteen chief officers, then follow Islip from boy monk to prior and abbot. His building work and public life close the story. The Dissolution waits just past the last page.
71734-the-biography-of-a-baby:
Milicent Washburn Shinn wrote the biography of a baby, copyrighted in 1900 at Boston. Her first chapter argues that the subjects nearest our hearts are the last to yield to scientific method. Babies grow in every household, yet the study of their minds, she says, has scarcely begun.

What is wanted, she holds, is a body of carefully observed facts, gathered with patience, honesty, and loving sympathy kept under restraint. Chapters follow her baby from the new-born's structure and sensations through grasping and handling things. The dawn of intelligence, creeping and standing, and the rudiments of speech lead to walking alone. Shinn helped found the study of child development.
72695-mammy-s-baby:
Amy Blanchard wrote the verses and Ida Waugh drew the pictures for this baby book of 1890. Worthington of New York copyrighted the picture book that year for the nursery. A baby eating and a baby in a dress open the illustrations at the front.

See how strong I am, the first poem's picture shows a baby with a cane. So strong are you, my baby, the verse answers in a mother's voice at the start. Soon the baby will lift chairs, mail letters and run errands, it promises, though mamma would like to keep her baby many a year, in a keepsake of Victorian babyhood.
74380-concerning-isabel-carnaby:
Concerning Isabel Carnaby is a novel by Ellen Thorneycroft Fowler, published by Appleton of New York in 1898. Fowler had written Cupid's Garden and two volumes of verses. A dedication in verse addresses her own people: kin, friends, and unknown readers who understand.

A prologue opens at a dinner in Grosvenor Square, at the house of Lord Kesterton, a new peer. Lady Eleanor Gregory asks whether he enjoys his honours, and he confesses he misses the Commons. Chapters follow Isabel through Childish Things, Esdaile Court, Elton Manor, and a place called Eden. Later titles promise indecision, expulsion from Eden, success, a state concert, and an election. Angus Grey and Joanna enter as chapters, and Life in London closes the list.
78294-the-golden-flutterby:
The Golden Flutterby is a story by Craig Rice, the pen name of Georgiana Ann Craig. She was magic, meant for love, its headnote says, and like so much beauty, strangely marked by fate. The tale is told long after, when barely a charred trace remains of the buildings that burned. A whole hillside of gay little houses once huddled down a steep valley from a broad avenue.

A man, now grown and settled, remembers it all and will never forget. It began on a windless, quiet night when he was young, lonely, and a stranger in town. Alone in a small shadowy bar, scarcely touching his glass, he saw her. She was golden from her braided hair to the gold slippers on her small feet. Her dress shone a deeper gold, and her skin seemed dusted with gold powder. Rice spins a wistful tale of beauty, chance, and fire.
78351-sitka-the-snow-baby:
Allen Chaffee wrote Sitka, the Snow Baby, published by the Milton Bradley Company in Springfield in 1923. Peter Da Ru, who knew and loved the Alaskan wilderness, drew the pictures. Chaffee had earlier written Unexplored and Lost River. The book joins the title story with a second tale, Finny-Foot, the Seal, and a glossary of Alaskan words.

Sitka is a polar bear cub who opens his eyes on a world of blue-white icebergs and green-blue ocean. He is as fat as butter and as fuzzy as a kitten, white so his enemies cannot see him plainly in the snow. Chapters bring Unga, an Eskimo boy, a drift on an iceberg, and a walrus herd. Summer blueberries and mosquitoes, wolves and salmon, and the birth of an iceberg follow. Chaffee writes true-to-life animal stories for children.
967-nicholas-nickleby:
Charles Dickens wrote this novel about Nicholas Nickleby, a young man who must support his mother and sister after his father's death. He takes a post at Dotheboys Hall, a cruel Yorkshire school run by Mr. Squeers, and he rescues Smike, a wretched pupil, before fleeing to London and the stage.

Dickens fills the tale with rogues and kind folk, from the Cheeryble brothers to the villainous Ralph Nickleby, Nicholas's uncle. The novel, begun soon after Pickwick, mixes comedy, melodrama, and social protest. Nicholas Nickleby remains a beloved Dickens story, of youth, honour, and the fight against cruelty.
affair-in-araby:
Affair in Araby is a 1922 adventure novel by Talbot Mundy, featuring his hero James Schuyler Grim, better known as Jimgrim. Jimgrim works as an American secret agent in British service, posted to Jerusalem. At his side are a loyal Sikh shadow, a fellow American, and a former Australian soldier, none of them shy of a fight.

Opportunity soon finds them in the unsettled Middle East of the postwar years. The book delivers a fast tale of intrigue and action in Arabia, built around Jimgrim's undercover work for British interests. It is one of Mundy's celebrated Jimgrim adventures, mixing espionage, travel, and battle in his popular manner.
britannica-1911-appleby:
Appleby, county town of Westmorland in England, is portrayed in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands in the valley of the Eden, 276 miles north west of London. The count in 1901 was 1764 people. Woods line the river, and fells rise to 2600 feet to the north east.

Above the town sits a castle with a fine Norman keep and a double moat. It was held for the royalists in the civil wars by Sir Philip Musgrave. Anne, countess of Pembroke, of the Clifford family, also lived there. She founded St Ann hospital for thirteen poor women in 1654. The text also notes a grammar school refounded by Queen Elizabeth.
britannica-1911-beverley-william-roxby:
William Roxby Beverley, an English artist and scene-painter, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was born at Richmond, Surrey, about 1814 and died in 1889. His father was an actor-manager who had taken the name Beverley. All four of his brothers and his sister also went on the stage.

Beverley worked as both actor and scene-painter from a young age. In 1831 his father and brothers took over the old Durham circuit of theatres. He joined them to play heavy comedy and to paint scenery. His work was first seen in London that same year. It was for a pantomime at the Victoria theatre. In 1853 he was named scenic director for the Covent Garden operas. The next year he entered the service of Drury Lane. The piece traces a stage craft passed down through one family.
britannica-1911-goby:
Goby is the name of a group of small fishes, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. Gobies are known by their lower chest fins being joined into one fin. That fin forms a sucking disk by which the fish can fix itself to rock. They are in the main coast fishes of nearly all seas.

Gobies thin out toward the Arctic and Antarctic oceans at both ends of their range. Many of them enter fresh waters near the sea, and some live in fresh water alone. Near 500 different kinds were known at the time of writing. The largest British kind, found in the rock pools of Cornwall, measures 10 inches in length. The males are in general more brightly coloured than the females and guard the eggs in a nest made from a shell.
britannica-1911-grimsby:
Grimsby, or Great Grimsby, is a borough and seaport of Lincolnshire, near the mouth of the Humber on its south shore. The 1911 Britannica entry gives it 63,138 people in 1901, and calls it an important seaport. St James's church, Early English and cruciform, stands in the older part of the town.

The port's modern story is docks. A reclamation and dock scheme begun by the railway in 1849 was completed in 1854, and extensions followed. Two large fish-docks serve a fleet of over 500 vessels, mostly steam trawlers, and the Royal and Alexandra docks take general traffic. A still larger dock was begun at Immingham in 1906. Butter, timber and cereals lead the imports; coal and woollen goods the exports. But the entry stresses that Grimsby is chiefly famous as a fishing port. Its early charters, from King John in 1201, fill the article's close.
britannica-1911-naseby:
Naseby is a town in Northamptonshire in England, south west of Market Harborough. It is famed as the place of a fight on the fourteenth of June in sixteen forty-five. That fight fixed the end of the first Civil War. The kings host was less than ten thousand strong.

The new host of the law house, led by Fairfax, was some three thousand more. The field is a wave ridge that parts two streams. At the first shock the kings foot broke most of the first line that faced it. A horse charge on one wing then ran too far in chase. Cromwell struck the core from the rear and sealed the win.
britannica-1911-porteus-beilby:
Beilby Porteus (1731–1808) was bishop of London, born at York. He was schooled at Christ's College, Cambridge, where he became a fellow in 1752. He was ordained in 1757 and in 1762 became a chaplain to the archbishop of Canterbury. In 1767 he became rector of Lambeth and took his doctor's degree at Cambridge. His sermon on that day led John Norris to set up a chair of divinity there.

About two years later Porteus became a chaplain to the king and master of the hospital of St Cross at Winchester. In 1776 he became bishop of Chester, and in 1787 he moved to London. He backed the Church Missionary Society and the British and Foreign Bible Society. He also worked for the end of slavery.
britannica-1911-ruby:
Ruby is a gem article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the most valued of all precious stones. The ruby, its name from the Latin rubeus, red, is a red, clear variety of corundum, crystallized alumina. It is sometimes called the oriental ruby to set it apart from the spinel ruby, a stone of less hardness, weight, and price.

The ruby grows in the hexagonal system and has no true cleavage, though it tends to split along certain gliding planes. Its colour runs from deep cochineal to pale rose red, at times with a tinge of purple. The tint men prize most has its own trade name. The article holds it unlikely that the true ruby was known to the ancient Hebrews, though the word stands in the English Old Testament.
britannica-1911-rugby:
Rugby, a market town in Warwickshire, England, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The town stands on high ground by the south bank of the Avon, near the Oxford Canal. Its urban district held 16,830 people in 1901, and rail lines made it a key junction north west of London.

Beyond the town's site and links, the entry gives much space to its famous boys' school. The school was founded under the will of Laurence Sheriff, a grocer and servant to Queen Elizabeth, who died in 1567. His gifts included land and a house in Rugby and a share of land in Middlesex. That London land, let for building, grew in time to yield about five thousand pounds a year.
britannica-1911-wallaby: A wallaby is a native name used for any member of one part of the kangaroo genus. Such animals have a bare muzzle and live in forests and dense scrub. They are sorted by size into large wallabies and small wallabies. Some of the small kinds are no bigger than a rabbit in size. From the places where they are found, they are also called brush kangaroos. The entry sends readers to the article on the kangaroo for the full account.
britannica-1911-whitby:
Whitby is a seaport, watering place, and market town in Yorkshire in England, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. It lies 245 miles north from London, on the North Eastern railway. Its count in 1901 was 11,755 for the urban district. It is beautifully situated at the mouth and on both banks of the River Esk.

The old town of narrow streets and pleasing houses stands on the steep slopes above the river. The modern residential quarter is mainly on the summit of West Cliff across the water. A long flight of steps leads up the eastern height to the abbey above the town. The ruins of that abbey gain a wonderful dignity from their commanding position, the text says. It was a foundation of Oswy, king of Northumbria, in 658, made in fulfilment of a vow for a victory over Penda of Mercia.
bruvver-jim-s-baby:
Philip Verrill Mighels wrote a mining-camp novel, printed by Harper and Brothers in 1904. Twenty-three chapters line the contents page. A Piute rabbit drive on a bright November day opens the tale. Old Jim and the camp of Borealis fill the cast.

A doll's making, a church bell, and Sunday doings in camp fill the early run. Christmas plans, a tree's making, and a full camp Christmas fill the heart of the book. A child in Jim's care — the Skeezucks of one chapter head — gets a name in the late run. Gold in Borealis, new folk in camp, and a parson's going mark the turns. Blizzard, a bed in the snow, and slate cleaning lead to a day of joy at the close. The book is given, with warm words, to the author's mother.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-whit:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Whitby, formerly Streoneshalh, describes a Benedictine monastery in Yorkshire's North Riding. Oswy, King of Northumberland, founded it about 657 as a double monastery. St. Hilda, its first abbess, ruled a community large enough to host the council of 664 that settled the Easter controversy.

On Hilda's death about 680, Aelfleda, Oswy's daughter, succeeded as abbess, and the house flourished until Danes destroyed it about 687, scattering the community. Abbot Titus fled to Glastonbury with Hilda's relics. No restoration was attempted until after the Norman Conquest. Whitby then passed to William de Percy, who refounded it late in the Conqueror's reign under Reinfrid, a monk of Evesham, as prior.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anthony-brook:
Anthony Brookby, also called Brorbey, was a Friar Minor and English martyr who died on 19 July 1537. At Magdalen College, Oxford, he lectured in divinity, knew Greek and Hebrew well, and enjoyed a reputation as an eloquent preacher. King Henry VIII took offence at a sermon in which Brookby attacked the king's actions and way of living, and at the king's command he was seized.

He was put to the rack and tortured in the cruellest manner to make him take back what he had said, but to no purpose. His tortures left him almost helpless, and a pious woman cared for him charitably for a fortnight. Then the king ordered an executioner to strangle him with his own Franciscan waist cord.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-willi:
William Filby, an English mission priest executed at Tyburn on 30 May 1582, shares this entry with fellow sufferers Luke Kirby and Laurence Richardson. Filby, an Oxfordshire man trained at Lincoln College and Reims, was ordained in 1581 and arrested within months. Kirby, a northern graduate reconciled at Louvain, was ordained at Cambrai in 1577 and seized at Dover in 1580. Richardson, a Brasenose fellow, was ordained in 1577 and worked in Lancashire.

All three endured long, harsh imprisonment. Filby was manacled from sentence to death and denied bedding for two months. Kirby was tortured with the Scavenger's Daughter and kept in irons. Richardson was held in Newgate and the Tower. Condemned together in November 1581, they died at Tyburn on 30 May 1582, a joint witness the entry records with full sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-ashby:
George Ashby, a Cistercian monk of Jervaulx in Yorkshire, was executed after the Pilgrimage of Grace in 1537. His name stands in several English martyrologies, yet its true form, and the place and manner of his death, remain uncertain. The rising's monks drew Henry VIII's fury, and soldiers were ordered to hang abbots and monks at once in their habits as a terrible example.

Whether Ashby died in the first vengeance or in June, when Abbot Adam Sedbergh was killed, no one can say. Stow seems to mean him by one Astbebe of Jervaulx who died with Sawley's abbot at Lancaster on March 10, 1537. The name may even come from Astleby, a pilgrim who visited Jervaulx. That Jervaulx monks died for rejecting Henry's schism is not disputed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-digby:
George Digby, second Earl of Bristol, was a Stuart courtier whose tongue cost him office after office. Born at Madrid in 1612, where his father was ambassador, he pleaded for his imprisoned father in Commons at twelve and took his Oxford degree in 1636. Elected for Dorset in 1640, he first backed Parliament, then broke with it over Strafford's attainder and joined the king in the Lords in 1641.

Digby advised seizing the five members, fought at Edgehill and Lichfield, and served as secretary of state in 1643 without success. Defeated in the north, he served France, inherited the earldom in 1653, and lost his secretaryship on converting to Catholicism in 1657. After the Restoration he opposed Clarendon, hid two years, and still backed the Test Act, splitting a Catholic of Rome's Church from one of Rome's Court.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-formby:
Henry Formby, born in 1816 into a Lancashire family that had lost the Catholic faith in the eighteenth century, was educated at Charterhouse and Brasenose College, Oxford. He became vicar of Ruardean in Gloucestershire. There he wrote A Visit to the East and a pamphlet on parochial psalmody. The Oxford Movement soon drew him on: after Newman's conversion he resigned his living and was received into the Catholic Church at Oscott in January 1846, being ordained priest the following year.

Formby's enduring interests were ecclesiastical music and illustrated religious teaching. At St. Chad's Cathedral he published works on plain chant and the Roman ritual and edited hymns for Catholic schools. He produced the very successful Pictorial Bible and Church History Stories, beginning in 1856, alongside illustrated lives of Benedict and Patrick. Retiring to Hinckley in 1864, he spent twenty more years issuing devotional and educational books before his death in 1884.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-abercrom: John Abercromby was a Scottish cleric said to have died for the Catholic faith in 1561, during the violence of the Scottish Reformation. Little is known for certain about him. The seventeenth-century writer Thomas Dempster names him among clergy who lost their lives in that persecution. The entry warns that Dempster's accuracy cannot always be trusted. He thinks Abercromby was a Benedictine who had written in defense of the faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kenelm-henry-:
Kenelm Henry Digby (1800-1880) was an Irish-born writer raised in a strongly Protestant family who became Catholic as a young man. This entry follows him from Trinity College, Cambridge, to a writing life devoted to the Middle Ages, which he called the Ages of Faith.

His best-known book, 'The Broadstone of Honour', first printed anonymously in 1822, treats the roots, spirit, and customs of Christian chivalry. A rewritten version ran to four volumes in 1826-27, with a five-volume luxury edition in 1876-77. 'Mores Catholici, or Ages of Faith', issued in eleven volumes between 1831 and 1840, ranges more widely over medieval Catholic life and thought.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-rigb:
An English priest who spent sixty years serving two Yorkshire missions, Nicholas Rigby anchors this short biographical entry. Born near Preston in 1800 and ordained in 1826, he settled at Ugthorpe, built its church in 1855, opened a new cemetery and started a middle-class college there.

Rigby handed his mission work to his curate around 1884 and died two years later. His writings receive a brief survey too, led by an 1834 book on church doctrine and Scripture, plus treatises on first truths and sermons of a disputing kind. His obituary in the Catholic Times of September 1886 sketches the same life in brief.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-risby:
Richard Risby was a Franciscan friar executed at Tyburn in 1534 for refusing Henry VIII's claim over the church. Born in the parish of St Lawrence, Reading, in 1489, he entered Winchester College in 1500 and later became a fellow of New College, Oxford. He gave up his fellowship in 1513 to join the Franciscan order, later serving as head of the Observant friary at Canterbury.

Condemnation came under an Act of Attainder alongside Elizabeth Barton, the so-called Holy Maid of Kent, and several other clergy. By a strange slip, his name was left out of a catalogue of those passed over in the act, while a pardoned man's name was wrongly included. A later Franciscan writer says Risby and another friar were twice promised life on condition they accept the king's supremacy. They refused, and Risby was executed on 20 April 1534.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-thime:
Richard Thimelby, also known as Ashby, was an English Jesuit missionary priest of the seventeenth century. Born in Lincolnshire in 1614, he entered the Society of Jesus in 1632. For about sixteen years he taught philosophy and theology at Liege. He was then posted to England, working chiefly in his home county.

Later posts took him back to the continent. In 1666 he became Master of Novices at Ghent. In 1672 he was named Rector of St Omer's in Belgium, where he remained until his death on 7 January that year. His writings were few: a translation of Father Binet's Treatise on Purgatory, later edited in 1874, and a controversial reply to Stillingfleet published in London in 1672.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-abercr:
Robert Abercromby was a Jesuit missionary whose most famous convert was Anne of Denmark, queen of James VI of Scotland. Born in 1532 and also known as Sanders and Robertson, he worked in secret among Scottish Catholics during the persecutions. Anne, raised a Lutheran, hated Calvinism and asked Catholic nobles for counsel. They sent her to Abercromby, who instructed her and received her into the Church about 1600.

James, warned of the conversion, told her to keep it secret lest it endanger his crown. He even made Abercromby Superintendent of the Royal Falconry so the priest could stay near the queen. Abercromby said Mass in secret at court and gave Anne communion several times. After James took the English throne, Anne refused the Protestant sacrament at the coronation, preferring to forfeit her crown. With 10,000 crowns on his head, Abercromby fled, and died at Braunsberg in Prussia in 1613.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-kilwar:
Robert Kilwardby was Archbishop of Canterbury and later a cardinal, a Dominican scholar who rose from the Paris schools. His birth is unknown; he studied at Paris and probably Oxford. For years he taught grammar and logic at Paris, pressing the use of the syllogism, and wrote many treatises. His De divisione scientiarum survives in many manuscripts.

Later he wrote theology, including works on Christ's passion and the sacrament of the altar, plus Scripture commentaries. Called to the Order of Preachers, he became a Dominican. He served as provincial of the order in England from 1261 to 1272. Gregory X then chose him for Canterbury, vacant for two years. As archbishop-elect he proclaimed Edward I king. Consecrated in February 1273, he visited his province, attended the Council of Lyons in 1274, and at Oxford in 1276 condemned errors and removed masters holding them. He died at Viterbo in 1279.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-everard-d:
Everard Digby, born 16 May 1578, died a traitor's death on 30 January 1606, aged only twenty-seven. He frequented Elizabeth's court, married Mary Mulsho in 1596, gaining a large fortune and two sons, Kenelm in 1603 and John in 1605. Raised a Protestant though his parents seem to have been Catholics, he met the Jesuit John Gerard about 1599, and both he and his wife converted.

In 1603 he welcomed James I at Belvoir Castle and was knighted that April. Yet he soon joined the Gunpowder Plot. His task was to prepare the rising that should follow the Westminster explosion. He rented Coughton Hall and staged a great hunting match on Dunsmore Heath for 5 November, to gather Catholic gentlemen as the nucleus of a rebel force. When Fawkes was seized, Digby rode with Catesby's desperate party, was captured at Holbeche on 8 November, pleaded guilty alone, and died first on the scaffold, protesting Gerard's innocence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-kenelm-di:
Kenelm Digby, physicist, naval commander, and diplomatist, was born at Gayhurst, Buckinghamshire, on 11 July 1603 and died in Covent Garden on 11 June 1665. Eldest son of Sir Everard Digby, executed for the Gunpowder Plot, he still inherited, after litigation, unconfiscated lands worth fifteen thousand pounds a year. In 1618 he entered Gloucester Hall, Oxford, under Thomas Allen, mathematician and occultist, whose books and manuscripts he later gave to the Bodleian.

Leaving Oxford without a degree in 1620, he loved Venitia Stanley, married her after his mother's opposition, and served the Prince of Wales in Spain. Knighted by James I, he later commanded a naval victory off Iskanderun. He mourned Venitia's sudden death in 1633 in two years of Gresham College seclusion, and left the Church before his 1636 reconciliation in France. Imprisoned by the Long Parliament, exiled, employed by Cromwell abroad, and restored at the Restoration, he joined the Royal Society's first council in 1663.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-john-rigby:
John Rigby, English martyr of 1600, confessed his faith while appearing for a sick recusant lady. Born about 1570 at Harrocks Hall, Eccleston, fifth or sixth son of Nicholas Rigby and Mary Breres of Preston, he served Sir Edmund Huddleston. When Huddleston's daughter, Mrs. Fortescue, ill, was cited to the Old Bailey for recusancy, Rigby appeared for her. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his execution at St. Thomas Waterings to 21 June 1600.

Compelled to confess himself Catholic, he was sent to Newgate. Next day, 14 February 1599 or 1600, he signed a confession. Reconciled by the martyr John Jones the Franciscan in the Clink two or three years before, he had since refused church. Chained to Newgate, then moved to the White Lion, he was tried on the first Wednesday of March. Offered a private chance to conform, he was sentenced next day for reconciliation, reprieved, and finally condemned on 19 June.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-synod-of-whit:
The Synod of Whitby in 664 settled whether England's Church would follow Rome or the Celtic tradition on Easter and much else. Augustine had begun Britain's conversion in 597, but Northumbria's missionaries came largely from Iona through Aidan, and English and Celtic customs clashed. King Oswy kept Easter while his queen, raised under Roman usage, still fasted, and the household discord grew extreme.

At Hilda's monastery, Oswy with Colman and Chad stood for the Celtic way, while Oswy's son Alchfrid with Wilfrid and Agilbert stood for Rome. Colman appealed to John, Wilfrid to Peter and Nicaea, and Oswy resolved not to offend Peter, keeper of heaven's doors. That choice linked England to Rome's rising organization rather than Ireland's declining Church, and the Western Easter dispute effectively ended there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-ashby:
Thomas Ashby suffered at Tyburn on 29 March 1544 for denying the king's supremacy over the Church. His name first reached the record of the English martyrs through chroniclers of the time, who noted his execution, and Sander repeated the account. Other Catholic writers did not carry it, and the Promoter of the Faith judged the proof too thin.

A later note in the Grey Friars' Chronicle calls Ashby a former priest who had left the priesthood, leaving his full position unclear. He may have rejected the royal supremacy without accepting the pope's authority. The entry weighs these scraps of evidence with care, showing why his case stayed doubtful among historians of the martyrs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-francis-i:
Francis Ingleby was an English martyr born about 1551, who suffered at York on Friday, 3 June 1586, old style. An early but inaccurate calendar gives 1 June. Fourth son of Sir William Ingleby of Ripley in Yorkshire and Anne Malory of Studley, he probably studied at Brasenose College, Oxford, in and before 1565. He joined the Inner Temple in 1576. On 18 August 1582 he reached the English College at Reims, where he lived at his own expense.

He was ordained subdeacon at Laon on Saturday, 28 May, deacon at Reims on Saturday, 24 September, and priest at Laon on Saturday, 24 December 1583. He left for England on Thursday, 5 April 1584, all dates new style. He laboured with great zeal around York, where he was arrested in the spring of 1586, tried for his priesthood, and executed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-william-a:
William Andleby was a Yorkshire priest executed at York in July 1597 after twenty years of secret ministry. Born at Etton, he went abroad at twenty-five to fight in the Dutch war and stopped at Douai to argue with Dr Allen. Converted overnight, he became a priest and served at a Lincolnshire household and among Catholic prisoners in Hull blockhouse.

For his first four years he travelled always on foot, meanly dressed, carrying his Mass vestments in a bag, because his work lay chiefly among the poor. Later, on his brethren's advice, he rode a horse and dressed somewhat better. His life was one of frequent fasting, watching, and continual prayer, so absorbed in God that he often failed to notice people he met. Condemned for his priestly character, he suffered with three laymen: John Abbot, Thomas Warcop, and Edward Fulthrop.
critical-strictures-on-the-new-tragedy-o:
A sharp attack on a new stage tragedy, Elvira by Mr David Malloch, fills this 1763 pamphlet. James Boswell, Andrew Erskine, and George Dempster wrote it together. The file is the Augustan Reprint Society edition, printed at Los Angeles in 1952 with an introduction by Frederick A. Pottle.

The three young Scots take the play apart scene by scene, in the mock grave style of the age. Their fun at Malloch's verse and plot made the piece a small classic of literary spite. Pottle's introduction sets out the facts of the quarrel. Readers get both the old pamphlet and modern notes on it. The book shows how fierce, and how witty, theatre fights could be in Georgian London.
doe-osti-2584746-bolt-pre-tensioning-in-:
Antonio Martin Recuero, Michael Tupek, and Alex Zeigle presented these slides at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory on July 8, 2025, filed as LLNL-TR-2009609. The deck is a step-by-step guide to a new bolt pre-tensioning feature in Diablo, the laboratory's solid mechanics simulation code. The feature gives users a more automated alternative to earlier approaches.

The slides first cover new print block features for postprocessing nodal, face, and element results, including a cutting plane capability. They then explain the pre-tension setup, how the Diablo solver iterates, and the preload keywords users must set. An application example works through vessel bolts in detail. Practical rules appear throughout, such as requiring the sidesets used for a bolt shank to be planar.
doe-osti-3023106-solutions-to-droop-and-:
James S Speck at the University of California, Santa Barbara, reports progress under award DE-EE0009691 for the period October 2021 through September 2025. His project attacks two linked weaknesses of long-wavelength LEDs: efficiency droop and the green gap. Green, yellow, and red III-nitride emitters have long lagged behind blue ones, which limits full-color lighting and displays.

The report blames poor material quality in high-indium InGaN quantum wells and the crystal's built-in polarization, which pulls electrons and holes apart and cuts light output. One fix redesigned the mirror and contacts so the distributed Bragg reflector wraps the whole mesa, with metal touching only its outer edge. The same wafer run through the old and new processes lets the team compare efficiency and wavelength directly.
from-yauco-to-las-marias-a-recent-campai:
Herrmann marched with the force he describes in this campaign history. He served in the Independent Regular Brigade under General Schwan. The brigade landed in Puerto Rico during the war with Spain. His chapters follow its march from Yauco inland. The first day ends in camp after hard marching. The people of the island get a chapter of their own.

Fighting comes at Hormigueros, where Spanish skirmishers open fire. Gatling guns and artillery answer from the fields. The brigade then occupies Mayaguez to an eager welcome. A final fight at Las Marias ends when news of the truce arrives. Herrmann closes with the district won and Schwan's farewell. The account is a participant's record, brisk and factual.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MannAbby_Mann_A: An FBI memorandum addressed to Mr. Sullivan is dated November 27, 1963, five days after the assassination. Copies went to Belmont, Rosen, and Callahan, all senior bureau officials. The body of the memo is garbled in the scan, so its subject cannot honestly be stated. What survives is the routing itself: proof that paper on the case was moving through the bureau's top offices while Dallas was still being investigated.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ShawAbbyFBISFPC: The FBI sent this airtel to Mr. DeLoach on October 31, 1969. Airtels to DeLoach, one of Director Hoover's closest aides, carried business meant for the top of the bureau. Most of this one's text is garbled in the scan, and its subject is not recoverable. What survives is the form and the date: a message from the field reaching the director's circle in the King case's second year, its contents lost to a bad copy.
greyfriars-bobby:
Eleanor Atkinson told the true Edinburgh legend in Greyfriars Bobby, her novel of a Skye terrier's faithfulness. Bobby comes to the Grassmarket in 1858 with Auld Jock, a Pentland farm laborer, and learns to love the one-o'clock gun from the castle because it means dinner. When Jock dies and is buried in Greyfriars kirkyard, the little dog will not leave the grave.

Atkinson builds her Edinburgh street by street: the Cowgate, George IV Bridge, the kirkyard on its hill, and the market folk who feed the dog they cannot adopt away from his post. Bobby kept his vigil for years, and Edinburgh later raised him a fountain. The novel is openly sentimental and carefully placed, a dog story anchored in a real city's stones.
john-enderby:
John Enderby is a historical tale by Gilbert Parker, set in Lincolnshire under King Charles. Enderby was among the strongest, proudest men the county gave to England, the opening says. The king came to Boston town on fen-draining business and other, more secret matters. There he tried to make Enderby a knight, against the man's own will.
